Both responses miss the point of the question. The user explicitly said "not LCA", and the highest common ancestor is the topmost shared ancestor, which is the root when both nodes are in the tree. Each assistant instead implemented the lowest common ancestor under a different name and never noted the ambiguity or the distinction.

**Assistant A:** This is the textbook LCA recursion, so it contradicts the "not LCA" instruction. It also has a correctness weakness. If only one of the nodes is in the tree, it returns that node instead of None. It includes no example or tests, and its explanation treats a node as its own ancestor without saying so.

**Assistant B:** It finds the root-to-node path for each target and returns the last shared node. That is also LCA, because the root-to-LCA prefix is the full common ancestor chain. The code is one line away from the correct "highest" answer, since the first element of the path is the root, but B didn't recognise this. On the plus side, it verifies that both nodes exist and returns None otherwise. It also includes a usage example, though the example's output of 2 confirms it is computing LCA. It searches by value rather than by node reference, which breaks with duplicate values, but that is a minor concern.

Both fail the central requirement. B is somewhat more robust (existence checking, example, clear structure), so it is marginally better.

[[B]]
